Notes:
Grade 11 DP English B class of six students (five boys and one girl), the teacher led a reading lesson on Chapter 8 of The Giver:
- Students had paper copies of the chapter and completed vocabulary work in context. 
- The teacher circulated to both tables to check for understanding, gave instructions, and brought the whole group together for clarification. 
- She checked synonyms with the class, used a slide on the screen to support vocabulary in context, commented on parts of the book, and asked students comprehension questions. 
- A short break was provided around 1:25 for water/bathroom.
Guiding Question1: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
Commendation1: Amy, you used Chapter 8 of The Giver to teach vocabulary in context, rather than in isolation. It supports DP Language B emphasis on developing receptive skills and understanding language as meaning-making. Checking synonyms with the whole group and using a visual slide also helped learners access challenging text, explicit literacy instruction.
Guiding Question2: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
Commendation2: You intentionally moved between both tables to monitor students' work, then gathered the class for whole group clarification. This balance of individual support and shared instruction reflects our emphasis on an inclusive learning environment, while supporting DP English B’s goal of developing confident readers and writers.
Commendation3: I wonder how we might increase students interactions during vocabulary and comprehension tasks like having them discuss synonyms or possible meanings with a partner before sharing with the groutp so as to further develop DP English B communication skills which will be used in oral assessment (IA). I also wonder if the brain break could be  in the classroom playing a board game or with music - this would help them not only with the brain break but also with the developemnet of lang B skills. Thanks a lot Amy!
Guiding Question3: To what extent do students apply what they learn to real-world contexts?
Response: Thank you for the feedback. My focus was on helping students access the chapter through vocabulary in context and checking their understanding as they worked. After the break, students shared their answers so they could consolidate their understanding of the vocabulary. I agree that adding partner discussion before whole-class sharing would give students more opportunities to explain their thinking and practice their speaking skills. Music or a short language game could be useful options for some breaks, although this break was intended to give students time to get water, use the bathroom, and reset.

You provided options for what to do if they had finished and provided reminders by lifting up the good exmaple first (i like how.....) Commendation3: Students' comments showed they recognized different emotions on each table and were wondering why that might be.  There were some comments showing they understood some of the contexts too. They clearly enjoyed thinking about this through familiar characters but I wonder how this will connect now to their own experiences and siutations and what they can do to manage the big emotions as they arise?  How do we encourage transfer from others to self?
Guiding Question3: How might this task shift students’ beliefs about their potential or their ability to influence outcomes in their lives?
Response:
Thank you for this thoughtful feedback! One of my goals for this lesson was to give students an opportunity to explore the four Zones of Regulation through familiar characters and real-life figures before connecting the learning to their own experiences. I wanted students to recognize that emotions can look different from person to person and that we cannot always tell how someone is feeling just by looking at them.

The inquiry activity took longer than I had anticipated, so we didn't get to the personal reflection I had originally planned. In our next guidance lesson, I plan to revisit the four Zones and have students complete a Guidance Journal reflection where they recall a time they experienced one of the Zones, identify how they were feeling, and describe what they noticed happening in their bodies. I think this is an important step in helping students move from recognizing emotions in others to developing awareness of their own emotional and physical cues.

From there, we will explore different regulation strategies and help students identify tools they can use when experiencing big emotions. I hope to help students understand that recognizing their Zone is only the first step; the next is learning to notice what they need and make choices about how to respond.

The transfer of SEL learning beyond guidance lessons has always been at the heart of my thinking. I believe the real impact happens when students begin recognizing their emotions and using strategies independently in authentic situations. I would love to continue exploring how we can reinforce this learning through consistent language and shared approaches across homerooms, specialist classrooms, playground supervision, hallway conversations, the lunchroom, and other situations. When students encounter the same language and expectations throughout their school day, I hope these skills become increasingly familiar and accessible when they need them most.

18 students were present. Students were seated at three long tables and were working on an ocean acidification activity using an online simulation and a paper worksheet. Joe was circulating around the room while students worked. At one point, he asked one student to return to their seat and continue with their work.

Students were using the PEEBEDU Ocean Acidification Simulator on their laptops. The simulation allowed students to change atmospheric CO? concentration and displayed changes in ocean conditions over time. Students could view real-time graphs for ocean pH, CO? concentration, calcium ion concentration, carbonate ion concentration and coral height. The simulation also displayed the condition of the coral. Students were asked to compare scenarios including atmospheric CO? concentrations of 280 ppm, 425 ppm and 600 ppm.

The accompanying worksheet included guided notes on gases dissolving in the sea and the chemistry associated with ocean acidification. Students were asked to make a prediction before using the model and then record patterns they observed under the different CO? scenarios. Later questions asked students to describe patterns in the pH and carbonate-ion graphs, use evidence from the simulation, explain the relationship using CO?, carbonic acid, H? ions and pH, and connect the chemistry to shell-building organisms and corals.

Joe stopped with two students to check their work and then continued circulating around the room. Some students were talking with others at their tables about the activity as they worked.

Joe asked one student what happened to the data when a variable was changed in the simulation and had the student show the change on the screen. He then asked a second student about carbonate. The student gave an answer that Joe identified as correct, and Joe followed up by asking the student to explain the answer in greater depth.

Joe then asked three students to answer questions connected to the activity. All three students were boys.
Guiding Question1: In what ways are students asked to take on an authentic societal role as part of their learning?
Commendation1: Joe, the ocean acidification simulation gave students a strong connection between the chemistry they were learning and an environmental issue with clear real-world significance. Students weren’t simply identifying what happened to pH or carbonate ions; they were manipulating atmospheric CO? levels, analysing the resulting data and then using that evidence to consider the impact on coral and other shell-building organisms. I particularly appreciated that the worksheet pushed students beyond observing the model to explaining what the evidence meant. This gave the activity some of the characteristics of how scientists use models and data to understand environmental change and its potential consequences, rather than the science remaining as an abstract chemistry exercise.
Guiding Question2: To what extent do students apply what they learn to real-world contexts?
Commendation2: Joe, there was a clear real-world connection in the way students were applying the chemistry of acids, pH and carbonate ions to ocean acidification. The simulation allowed them to change atmospheric CO? levels and then see what that meant for ocean chemistry and coral health, including comparing current conditions with both historical and future scenarios. I appreciated that students were then asked to use the data they generated to explain those relationships rather than simply observe what happened on the screen. It was a useful opportunity for students to see how the chemistry they are learning can help them understand an environmental issue beyond the classroom.
Commendation3:
Joe, thanks for having me in your class. One thing I found myself thinking about was where student voice and choice can realistically sit within a science curriculum like this. There is clearly core scientific knowledge that all students need to develop, and I don’t think personalization necessarily means creating completely different pathways through that content. The ocean acidification work, though, feels like an interesting opportunity because the science connects to environmental changes that affect different places and communities in very different ways.

I wonder whether, once students have developed the common scientific understanding, there could occasionally be space for them to choose where they take that learning next. For example, students might investigate the implications for a place, ecosystem, food source, industry or community that has some connection to their own experiences, interests or cultural background. That could preserve the common science learning while giving students some ownership over the context in which they apply it. It may also create opportunities for students to bring knowledge and perspectives into the classroom that you wouldn't necessarily be able to plan for yourself.

Where within a fairly content-driven science curriculum could you intentionally create small points of choice that allow students to connect the common science learning to places, issues or experiences that have particular meaning for them?
Guiding Question3: How might we ensure students are given voice and choice in the curriculum to reflect their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences?
Response:
This was the third lesson in the sequence on ocean acidification.  In the previous 2 lessons we discussed things such as the periodic table, the conservation of mass, ions, balancing equations.  Today's activity was one in which I treated as a bridge to the next class where we are going to do more hands on science and collect real data.  This activity had the student simulate 3 different times in history where there were different levels of carbon dioxide in the air.  I like this simulation because it is scaffolded well.  At the base level, the students can make observations about the dissolved ions, the amount of carbonic acid formed, and the subsequent growth of the corals in the ocean.  For students that wanted to dig a little deeper into the data, there is a link in the graph where they can download the data themselves and get a more fine grained look at some of the numbers (I was happy to have Anyan do just that!!). 
I really enjoy this unit.  It lends itself very nicely to real world connections and applications.  I like that it takes a real world situation (climate change, ocean acidification) and connects it to the theory we discuss and read about in class, 
 
Going forward, the kids will be able to have more personalization in their learning when it comes time to their criterion B and C assignments.  While I will choose the general experiment to be run, they will be the ones who choose the independent variable to change and the dependent variable to measure.  
As a side note, I use random calling during class and during that small time during the visit, the names called were boys.  During the rest of the class, there was a more gendered mix of students called.

Notes:
21 students were present. Students were divided into four groups and were working on gymnastics routines on mats in the gym. The groups were separated by gender, with boys and girls working in different groups.

Students were practising and developing a planned group routine. Each group was working around a sequence they had previously planned, with students talking together and physically trying different movements and positions on the mats.

The displayed goals for Lesson 4 were to add transition movements between all holds, complete the routine sequence, add challenging whole-group holds to the routine, and complete an ATL assessment.

Planning materials showed that the sequence of lessons had moved from individual holds and transitional movements, to small-group and whole-group holds, and then to performance planning. The activity required students to include one individual hold, one transition move and one small- or whole-group hold before combining these movements with the other members of their group to construct one continuous routine.

Groups had paper planning sheets with diagrams and annotations showing different positions, holds and sequences. Students were using these plans while working on their routines on the mats.

During the observation, each group was working around its planned routine, with students discussing what they were going to do and practising sections of the sequence together. Diego was continually circulating and supervising the groups.
Guiding Question1: To what extent does creative expression foster empathy and compassion among students?
Commendation1: Diego, I appreciated the creative thinking that students were having to do as they developed their gymnastics routines together. Each group had a plan, but they were also physically trying things out, talking through ideas and working out how the different holds and transitions could fit together. What stood out to me was that creating the routine wasn’t only about what an individual student could do. They had to consider what other members of the group were comfortable and able to do, adapt their ideas when something didn’t work, and find a way for everyone to be part of the final routine. In a PE setting, where students can have very different levels of confidence and physical ability, I thought this was a nice example of creativity requiring students to be aware of and responsive to one another.
Guiding Question2: How are strong, trusting relationships cultivated as the foundation for peer learning and conflict resolution?
Commendation2: Diego, the group routine gave students a genuine reason to work together rather than collaboration simply being part of the structure of the lesson. I noticed groups talking through their plans, trying movements together and making adjustments as they worked out how to connect the different parts of their routine. There was also a level of trust required in some of the group holds, where students were physically relying on one another to make the movement work safely. I appreciated that students had the time and space to work through this together rather than you directing each group towards a solution. It meant that listening, negotiating and trusting one another were necessary parts of successfully completing the task.
Commendation3:
Diego, thanks for having me in your class. One thing I found myself thinking about during the lesson was whether PE can intentionally help students change the way they see themselves. Some students arrive in PE already believing that they aren’t athletic, aren’t coordinated, or simply aren’t “PE people.” For students who feel more successful in academic spaces, or who may be uncomfortable with their bodies or with physical performance in front of others, those beliefs can become quite fixed.

The gymnastics work felt like an interesting opportunity to challenge some of that. Success wasn’t simply about being the fastest or strongest student; there were different ways to contribute to the group routine, and students had the opportunity to practise something, adjust it and see themselves improve. I wonder how intentionally we make that growth visible, particularly for the students who might need to see it most. If students can leave a unit thinking, “I couldn’t do that before, but now I can,” that feels like an important experience of personal change. Over time, those experiences might also help students see movement and physical activity as something that belongs to them, regardless of whether they ever identify as an athlete.

How might you intentionally help students who come into PE with a fixed belief about their own physical ability recognise evidence that they can change, improve and become more confident through movement?
Guiding Question3: Does this experience help students believe that change - personal or societal - is possible?
Response:
I think it starts with helping students recognise their own progress rather than comparing themselves to others. In PE, some students already believe they are not athletic or capable, and I want to challenge that thinking by creating opportunities for small successes.

I could be more intentional about having students set personal goals, reflect on their progress, and recognise what they can do now that they couldn't do before. Acrogymnastics is a great example because students can contribute in different ways and experience success at their own level.

I also want to focus my feedback more on effort, improvement, and willingness to try. Ultimately, I want students to understand that physical ability can develop and that PE is for everyone, not just those who identify as athletes.

Notes:
15 students were present, seated individually or in small groups at desks. Students were working on Criterion C: Creating the Solution, with students at different stages of completion.

Students were developing mini house models. Cardboard models were visible on desks, with students constructing walls, roofs, windows and other parts of their designs. Some models had measurements and labels written directly onto the cardboard, including dimensions for walls, windows and other features. Masking tape was being used to join different sections of the models.

Students were also working on their Criterion C documentation on their laptops. The C1 task required students to outline a plan that considered the use of resources and time and was detailed enough for a peer to follow to create the solution. The planning table included the steps/process, resources and tools/materials, and time to complete or due date. Students had begun recording individual construction steps in their plans.

There was a range of progress across the class. Some students were working on their physical models while others were working on the digital planning/documentation connected to the task.

Students talked with one another about their work while at their desks. Seba circulated around the room, stopping with students to support them and answer questions. He also answered questions about the digital tools and the steps students were working through.
Guiding Question1: In what ways does the learning environment support risk-taking?
Commendation1: Seba, the learning environment you created gave students genuine space to take risks with their ideas and work through the design process rather than simply trying to reproduce the same solution. I particularly appreciated seeing the variety in the models around the room. Students were all working within the same Criterion C expectations, but the solutions themselves looked quite different, and they were at different stages of making, testing and documenting their work. There was also something valuable about the physical nature of the task: cardboard, tape, measurements and partially completed models meant that students could try something, see whether it worked, and then make adjustments. Your circulation around the room and the individual support you provided also meant students had access to you without you taking over that process. This felt like a learning environment where there was room for experimentation and for a solution not to be perfect on the first attempt.
Guiding Question2: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
Commendation2:
Seba, students had a good level of ownership over how they were progressing through the design process. I could see this particularly in the variety of completion points around the room and in the conversations students were having as they worked through their own models and Criterion C documentation. They were making decisions about the sequence of their work, the construction of their individual solution, and how they documented the process rather than waiting for you to direct each next step.

There were also some clear Tier 1 supports sitting underneath that independence. The Criterion C planning structure gave everyone a common framework for breaking the process into manageable steps, identifying resources and materials, and thinking about timelines, while the physical models gave students an immediate visual reference for what they had already completed and what still needed attention. You were then able to circulate and provide individual support where needed without that becoming the primary way students accessed the task. That combination of clear universal structure and space for individual decision-making supported students to manage their own progress and make meaningful decisions about their learning.
Commendation3:
Seba, thanks for having me in your class. I liked the balance in this lesson between having a clearly defined task and giving students the space to work through it at their own pace. Everyone was clearly working towards the same Criterion C expectations, but there was already quite a lot of individuality in the solutions being created.

One thing I wondered about was whether there could be an opportunity to push that individuality further by deliberately inviting students to draw on their own cultural backgrounds, experiences or understanding of what makes a home. A task like this potentially lends itself really well to that. Ideas about homes and living spaces can look very different depending on where someone has lived, who they live with, cultural traditions, climate, family needs or simply what they personally value in a space. It could be interesting for students to make some of those choices intentionally and then be able to explain why their solution looks the way it does, rather than personalization being primarily about the design choices they make within the assigned task.

How might you create space within a common design brief for students to bring something of their own identity, culture or lived experience into the problem they are solving, and make those choices an intentional part of their design thinking?
Guiding Question3: How might we ensure students are given voice and choice in the curriculum to reflect their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences?

Notes:
19 students were present for a climbing wall lesson. Students were gathered outside at the climbing wall, with some students wearing climbing harnesses. Students took turns climbing while other students remained at the base of the wall.

During the observation, one student was near the top of the climbing wall while another student was climbing lower down. Several students were involved with the ropes at the base of the wall. Students waiting for their turn were standing or sitting on the mats near the climbing area.

Sharon was positioned near the climbing wall and was supervising students as they climbed. A substitute teacher was also assisting with the lesson and was identified as an experienced climber.

One student became stuck while climbing and called down from the wall. Another student joined the rope and began belaying, which allowed the student on the wall to continue. At another point, one student was coming down from the wall.

Sharon asked students at the end of their climb how they felt about the climb and the level they had reached.

One student was using crutches and did not participate in the climbing activity during the observation.

The class also included work connected to interpersonal skills. One group returned their harnesses to the equipment room while another two groups continued at the climbing wall. Sharon then sent students to change in the locker room.
Guiding Question1: Does this experience help students believe that change - personal or societal - is possible?
Commendation1:
Sharon, the climbing lesson gave students a really tangible experience of personal change. I particularly appreciated that students were working at different points on the wall and that the focus wasn’t simply on reaching the top. When students finished a climb, you asked them how they felt about it and about the level they had reached, creating an opportunity for them to recognise their own progress and experience.

Climbing is also an activity where progress is very visible. A student can be unsure about leaving the ground, struggle with a particular section, or need support from the people below, and then experience themselves moving beyond that point. I saw a nice example of this when one student became stuck and, with another student joining the belay, was able to continue. Those experiences can help students see that their current ability or confidence isn’t necessarily fixed, and that challenge, support and persistence can allow them to do something they may not initially have thought they could do.
Guiding Question2: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
Commendation2:
Sharon, there was a nice element of reflection built into the climbing experience. I particularly appreciated that when students finished their climb, you asked them how they felt and how they thought they had done. You also asked students about the interpersonal skills they had used during the activity, which extended that reflection beyond their individual physical performance to how they had worked with and supported others. It was a simple interaction, but it shifted some of the responsibility for evaluating the experience back to the students rather than you immediately telling them whether the climb had been successful.

That feels particularly valuable in an activity like climbing, where progress is very individual and success also relies heavily on other people. Reaching a particular height might represent very different things for different students depending on their previous experience, confidence and goals, while belaying and supporting a climber require communication, trust and responsibility. Giving students the opportunity to reflect on both their own progress and the interpersonal skills they used helped them think more broadly about what successful participation in the lesson looked like.
Commendation3:
Sharon, thanks for having me in your class. One thing I found myself thinking about during the climbing was how personalization works in an activity that is intentionally physically challenging. Students are coming into an experience like this with very different levels of strength, confidence and previous experience. For some students, getting higher on the wall might be the obvious challenge; for others, simply attempting a route, trusting the equipment, supporting someone else or taking on a role within the group might represent significant progress.

I wonder if there is an opportunity to make those different pathways to success even more explicit for students. The questions you were already asking students about how they felt after their climb and the interpersonal skills they had used could provide a really natural starting point. Rather than success being defined primarily by how high someone climbs or how effectively they can perform a particular physical role, students could perhaps identify what challenge, contribution or area of growth is meaningful for them within the experience. That could be particularly valuable for students who don't initially see climbing, or even PE more generally as an area of strength or interest.

How might you help students identify their own meaningful challenge or way of contributing within a physically demanding activity, so that every student can see a pathway towards genuine progress and success without removing the challenge that makes the experience valuable?
Guiding Question3: In what ways are students have opportunities to pursue their interests and passions?
Response: Hi John, Thank you for the feedback. Personalization in climbing is something I think about carefully, because students come in with very different levels of confidence and experience. For that reason, I don't use height as the main measure of success in this unit. What I'm looking for is whether students are demonstrating the technique we're focusing on; things like footwork, body positioning, and communication with their belayer. Students also rotate through routes of different difficulty levels, so there's always both a challenge and an opportunity to experience success, rather than one fixed goal of reaching the top. Reflection is built into the lesson deliberately. When students finish a climb, I ask how they felt and how they think they did, rather than immediately evaluating for them. I also ask about the interpersonal skills they used, so they're thinking about how they supported others, not just how they performed individually. Mid-unit, students complete a self-reflection where they analyse their own technique against teaching cues, identify what's working and what to improve, then return to the wall with a specific focus. Interpersonal skills are assessed separately through Criterion Di, which creates a genuine second pathway for students who find the physical climbing more difficult.  For example during the unit, the students with crutches, rather than sitting out, she tracked the goals each climber had set and the panels they actually reached for her group. That was a meaningful contribution to the group and a real demonstration of the skills Criterion Di assesses. I plan to name the technique or role focus at the beginning of each lesson and use reflection prompts like "What technique improved?", "What felt challenging?" in addition to "How did you support someone else?" so every student can identify something personally meaningful to work towards, without removing the challenge that makes the experience worthwhile. Thank you for stopping by.
